title: Carbohydrates Structure
objectives: Understand the structure and classification of carbohydrates
Describe the chemical properties and reactions of monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides
Explain the biological roles of carbohydrates in energy storage and cell recognition
Analyze the significance of carbohydrate derivatives in metabolic pathways

overview.title: Carbohydrate Overview
overview.content:
Carbohydrates (CHO) are organic compounds composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, typically with a hydrogen to oxygen ratio of 2:1. They are classified into monosaccharides (simple sugars), disaccharides (two monosaccharides linked together), and polysaccharides (long chains of monosaccharides). Carbohydrates serve as a primary energy source, structural components in cells, and play key roles in cell-cell recognition and signaling.

Biological Significance

  • Energy Source: Glucose is a major fuel for cells, broken down via glycolysis to produce ATP.
  • Structural Role: Cellulose in plants and chitin in arthropods provide rigidity and support.
  • Cell Recognition: Glycoproteins and glycolipids on cell surfaces mediate immune responses and cell adhesion.
  • Storage: Glycogen in animals and starch in plants store glucose for later use.

Key Features

Monosaccharides

  • Glucose (aldohexose)
  • Fructose (ketohexose)
  • Galactose (aldohexose)
  • Ribose (aldopentose)

Disaccharides

  • Sucrose (glucose + fructose)
  • Lactose (glucose + galactose)
  • Maltose (glucose + glucose)

key_concepts.title: Key Concepts
key_concepts.content:
Isomerism in Carbohydrates

Definition: Monosaccharides exhibit structural, stereoisomerism (D/L forms), and anomerism (α/β forms).

Example: D-glucose and L-glucose are enantiomers; α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose are anomers.

Glycosidic Bonds

Definition: Covalent bonds formed between hydroxyl groups of two monosaccharides, releasing water (dehydration synthesis).

Example: α-1,4-glycosidic bond in maltose; β-1,4-glycosidic bond in cellulose.

Reducing vs. Non-Reducing Sugars

Definition: Reducing sugars have free aldehyde or ketone groups (e.g., glucose, maltose); non-reducing sugars do not (e.g., sucrose).

Test: Benedict's reagent detects reducing sugars by forming a colored precipitate.

chemical_reactions.title: Chemical Reactions
chemical_reactions.content:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation: Aldehyde group of sugars can be oxidized to carboxylic acids (e.g., glucose → gluconic acid).

Reduction: Sugars can be reduced to sugar alcohols (e.g., glucose → sorbitol).

Hydrolysis

Process: Breakdown of disaccharides/polysaccharides into monosaccharides by adding water.

Example: Sucrose + H2O → Glucose + Fructose (catalyzed by sucrase).

Maillard Reaction

Process: Non-enzymatic browning reaction between reducing sugars and amino acids.

Significance: Important in food chemistry (e.g., browning of bread).

biological_roles.title: Biological Roles
biological_roles.content:
Energy Metabolism

Glycolysis: Glucose is catabolized to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH.

Glycogenolysis: Glycogen is broken down into glucose-1-phosphate for energy.

Structural Components

Cellulose: Provides rigidity to plant cell walls.

Chitin: Forms exoskeletons of arthropods and fungal cell walls.

Cell Signaling

Glycoproteins: Cell surface markers (e.g., blood group antigens).

Heparin: Acts as an anticoagulant.

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
What is the difference between starch and cellulose?+
Starch (α-1,4 and α-1,6 bonds) is energy storage in plants; cellulose (β-1,4 bonds) is a structural component.
Why is fructose sweeter than glucose?+
Fructose's ring structure interacts more strongly with sweet taste receptors.
How do carbohydrates contribute to blood types?+
Blood group antigens (A, B, O) are determined by specific carbohydrate structures on red blood cell surfaces.
What is the role of glycogen in the liver?+
Glycogen is stored in the liver and broken down into glucose to maintain blood sugar levels.
